conclusion.label: Most likely cause
conclusion.text: The Aldergate T1 345 kV bushing's condenser core is deteriorating

series.label: Aldergate T1 bushing C1 power factor

chart.title: What we see
chart.caption: C1 power factor on the Aldergate T1 345 kV bushings against their own first-hour baseline. The shaded gap is the rise.

checks.label: Power factor well above its own baseline
checks.value: C1 power factor 0.956 % now against 0.374 % in the first hour (+0.582 points, 2.6× baseline). Alert level is +0.10 points.
checks.why: Power factor measures the losses in the bushing's paper-and-oil insulation. Moisture or partial discharge in the condenser core raises it. The baseline is this bushing's own, so its nameplate value doesn't matter.

checks.label: Rising steadily, not jumping
checks.value: +0.125 points per hour over the last 2 h. Largest 5-min step since 09:45: 0.016 points.
checks.why: Insulation deteriorates progressively. A monitor or wiring fault usually shows as a step.

checks.label: Sustained, not a passing excursion
checks.value: More than +0.10 points since 10:15 (3 h 50 min); above +0.03 since 09:45.
checks.why: Needs 30 min above the alert level, so a humidity or temperature swing on the reading doesn't raise an item.

checks.label: Capacitance rising with it
checks.value: Capacitance deviation 0.52 % in the first hour, 4.19 % now (+3.67 points). Investigate level is 5 %.
checks.why: A separate quantity from the same tap. Shorted grading layers raise capacitance; a surface or temperature effect on the power factor reading does not.

checks.label: Leakage current up
checks.value: 43.3 mA in the first hour, 59.7 mA now (+37.8 %).
checks.why: More capacitance and more loss both draw more current through the insulation at the same voltage.

checks.label: Every other bushing flat
checks.value: The other 10 bushing sets stayed within ±0.014 points of their own baselines all day.
checks.why: Ambient temperature and humidity reach every bushing in the fleet. Only this one moved.

checks.label: Transformer load and oil normal
checks.value: Aldergate T1 at 68 % of nameplate; top oil 64.6 °C, 0.3 °C from Aldergate T2 at the same load.
checks.why: Bushing power factor rises with temperature. With the load and the oil where they should be, the change is in the insulation.

references.title: Grading layers shorting in the core
references.description: Partial discharge or moisture shorts the foil layers one after another. Power factor and capacitance climb together and speed up; the bushing comes out before it fails.
notes: Power factor and capacitance rising together, as here
Capacitance up 3.7 points in 4 h 20 min

references.title: Moisture ingress, no layers shorted yet
references.description: Water through a failed gasket raises the losses, so power factor climbs, but capacitance holds until layers start to short.

verdict.text: Earlier stage of the same failure

notes: Here capacitance is already moving, so it is past this stage
Same test confirms either

references.title: Temperature swing on the reading
references.description: Uncorrected power factor follows oil and ambient temperature through the day and comes back down overnight. Capacitance doesn't move and every bushing on the site does the same.
notes: The other 10 bushing sets stayed flat through the same heat
Here capacitance moves too

ruledOut.reason: Aldergate T1 DGA: acetylene 0.37 ppm (−0.02), ethylene 19.8 ppm, combustible gas rate 2.6 ppm/day (1.1× its first hour). Hydrogen crept up 7 ppm, which is present but not a fault pattern. The bushing core has its own oil, separate from the tank.
Aldergate T1 at 68 % of nameplate, top oil within 0.3 °C of Aldergate T2, whose bushings stayed flat.
Power factor, capacitance and leakage current all moved, gradually and in the direction shorted layers produce. A failed tap adapter or monitor input jumps, or moves one quantity.
Dirt or moisture on the outside can raise online power factor on a humid day. The offline test with a guard lead separates surface from core.

confidence.because: Power factor, capacitance and leakage current, three quantities from the bushing monitor, moved together, gradually, while every other bushing and the transformer's own load and oil stayed normal.
confidence.notHigherBecause: Nobody has tested the bushing offline yet, and the online monitor can't separate a surface effect from the core.
confidence.raiseIf: The Doble test at the outage shows power factor and capacitance up against nameplate and the sister phases.
confidence.lowerIf: The offline test, corrected to 20 °C, reads close to nameplate. Then look at the monitor and the surface.

action.text: Doble power factor and capacitance test at the next outage window, corrected to 20 °C and compared against nameplate and the sister phases. Treat monitored evolution as unpredictable: documented cases run from ten days of warning down to minutes.

GSIT01.impact: At the last hour's rate (+0.126 points/h) power factor reaches 1.0 % (remove at the next outage) in about 21 min and 2.0 % (don't wait for one) in about 8 h 18 min. Monitored failures have come anywhere from ten days to minutes after a trend like this.

conclusion.label: Most likely cause
conclusion.text: A developing thermal fault (overheating, not arcing) inside Kessler T2

chart.title: What we see
chart.caption: Dissolved combustible gas rate on Kessler T2 against its own first hour and its sister bank Kessler T1. The 30 ppm/day action level is well above this chart.

checks.label: Gas rate multiplied
checks.value: TDCG rate 9.02 ppm/day now against 2.12 ppm/day in the first hour (4.2×). Above 2× since 10:20.
checks.why: Combustible gases dissolve in the oil when something inside overheats or arcs. The rate at which they build up matters more than the total.

checks.label: Still rising
checks.value: +1.25 ppm/day per hour over the last 2 h; rising since about 09:15.
checks.why: A developing hot spot makes gas faster as it grows. A one-off event leaves a step and a flat rate.

checks.label: Sustained for hours
checks.value: Above 2× its baseline for 3 h 45 min.
checks.why: Needs 1 h, so an oil-temperature swing through the monitor doesn't raise it.

checks.label: Hydrogen and ethylene rising
checks.value: Hydrogen 34.7 → 90.0 ppm, ethylene 15.4 → 41.6 ppm since the first hour. TDCG +148 ppm in 6 h 5 min, which on its own would be about 584 ppm/day: faster than the monitor's rate says. One of the two figures is wrong, and only a lab sample can say which.
checks.why: Separate gas channels. Ethylene with hydrogen is the signature of overheated oil and paper (thermal fault); the rate figure alone can't say what kind of fault it is.

checks.label: No acetylene
checks.value: Acetylene 0.27 ppm in the first hour, 0.27 ppm now.
checks.why: Acetylene needs an arc, above about 700 °C. Without it the fault is thermal, not a discharge.

checks.label: Moisture flat
checks.value: Moisture in oil 6.2 → 6.1 % saturation.
checks.why: Wet oil or a leak would move moisture. It didn't, so the gas isn't coming from a breathing or sealing problem.

checks.label: Other transformers flat
checks.value: The other 10 monitors' rates are 0.96–1.10× their own first hour, through the same hot day.
checks.why: The afternoon heat reaches every transformer. Only this one started making gas.

references.title: Overheated joint or blocked duct (thermal fault)
references.description: A loose lead connection or a blocked cooling duct cooks the oil and paper around it. Hydrogen, methane and ethylene build over days to weeks; acetylene stays near zero.
notes: Rate climbing, acetylene flat, as here
Weeks-long in reality: today shows only the start

references.title: Low-energy arcing
references.description: A floating shield or poor contact sparks. The rate rises the same way, but acetylene appears from the start.
notes: Acetylene here moved +0.00 ppm
Arcing would call for a faster outage

references.title: Online monitor drifting
references.description: A monitor's sensor or calibration drifts and the reported rate creeps up. The lab sample drawn the same day reads normal.

verdict.text: Not ruled out until the lab sample

notes: Individual gases moving in a thermal-fault pattern argue against drift
The rate and concentration figures disagree with each other

ruledOut.reason: Acetylene 0.27 ppm, +0.00 since the first hour.
Kessler T1, the same design at the same station, carried 94 % at its peak today against 81 % here, and its gas rate stayed at 2.33 ppm/day. The rise here began at 09:15, before the afternoon load.

ruledOut.cause: Tap changer oil leaking into the main tank
ruledOut.reason: The tap changer compartment stayed 5.5–6.4 °C cooler than the main tank. A leaking diverter adds acetylene too.
Separate gas channels rose in a thermal pattern, which a single drifting sensor rarely does, but the rate and the concentrations disagree. Only the laboratory sample settles it.

confidence.because: The rate has more than doubled and is still rising, hydrogen and ethylene climbed on their own channels, and acetylene stayed flat, which is the thermal-fault pattern.
confidence.notHigherBecause: This is one online monitor, and its rate and its concentrations don't agree with each other. No laboratory sample yet.
confidence.raiseIf: The lab resample confirms the gases, and a Duval triangle places them in a thermal zone.
confidence.lowerIf: The lab sample shows today's concentrations flat. Then it is the monitor.

action.text: Resample from the main tank within 24 hours and confirm the rate rather than the absolute values. Run Duval triangle on the confirmed sample. Keep T2 loaded normally meanwhile.

GSIT02.impact: At +1.25 ppm/day per hour the monitor's rate would be about 21 ppm/day by midnight, still under the 30 ppm/day action level. The concentrations, if the lab confirms them, would already be past it.

conclusion.label: Most likely cause
conclusion.text: The Larkspur 138 kV bus CVT's capacitor stack is failing; the bus voltage was never low

series.label: Larkspur 138 kV bus voltage in SCADA

chart.title: What we see
chart.caption: Change from the first hour, in %, for the CVT's secondary voltage, the bus voltage in SCADA, and the buses at the far end of its circuits. Only the CVT walked away.

checks.label: Disagrees with the redundant measurement
checks.value: 6.12 % apart now, against 0.24 % in the first hour. Over 2 % since 10:00, past the 5 % alarm at 11:35.
checks.why: The two relays on this bus should read the same voltage. The alarm point, 5 % (0.05 pu), is the published redundant-measurement check.

checks.label: Nothing else saw the voltage change
checks.value: CVT output −6.2 % from its first hour; the SCADA bus voltage −1.4 %, and Wyndham 138 kV bus −1.6 %, Orrin 138 kV bus −1.1 % and Wexford 138 kV bus −1.3 %. The SCADA bus voltage's own steps today (−1.9 % at 09:40 and −5.8 % at 10:15) showed on its neighbours in the same scan; the CVT's drift never did.
checks.why: A real voltage change moves every measurement of it together, here and one circuit away. An instrument fault moves one.

checks.label: The CVT's capacitance changed
checks.value: Capacitance deviation 0.31 % in the first hour, 2.91 % now. A healthy stack stays within 2 % of nameplate.
checks.why: A separate measurement of the capacitor stack itself. Shorted elements change the divider ratio and the capacitance at the same time.

checks.label: Its power factor rose
checks.why: Damaged or wet elements add loss in the stack.

checks.label: Kept out of voltage control
checks.value: Block Larkspur bus CVT as a voltage control source: done at 12:10. The deviation has held flat since.
checks.why: If the tap changer believes a low reading it raises the real voltage to "fix" it. Removing the input stops a sensor fault becoming a control problem.

references.title: Capacitor elements shorting in the stack
references.description: Elements in the high-voltage stack short one by one. The ratio drifts over hours; the other relay and the bus stay where they were, and the CVT's capacitance moves.
notes: Gradual drift, bus flat, as here
Capacitance up 2.6 points here

references.title: Blown secondary fuse or open wiring
references.description: The same "only one measurement moved" pattern, but all at once: the reading steps to near zero in one scan and the capacitance doesn't change.
notes: Here the drift took hours
Here the capacitance moved

references.title: A real voltage sag
references.description: A real sag moves every measurement of the bus together and the buses nearby too. The two relays still agree, so the deviation stays flat.
notes: Here the deviation grew while the bus stayed put
Neighbouring buses didn't follow

ruledOut.cause: A real voltage drop on the bus
ruledOut.reason: The SCADA bus voltage is −1.4 % from its first hour against the CVT's −6.2 %, and Wyndham 138 kV bus, Orrin 138 kV bus and Wexford 138 kV bus didn't follow.
Those fail as a step, and they don't change the stack's capacitance. This drifted for 2 h 30 min and the capacitance moved.

ruledOut.cause: The other relay is the one that's wrong
ruledOut.reason: The redundant measurement agrees with the bus voltage in SCADA and with the neighbouring buses. Every other CVT in the fleet stayed within 0.46 % of its partner.
Ferroresonance shows as distorted, oscillating output, often after switching. This is a smooth, one-way drift.

confidence.because: Only this CVT moved: the other relay, the SCADA bus voltage and the buses one circuit away all held, and the CVT's own capacitance changed the way shorted elements change it.
confidence.notHigherBecause: Nobody has tested the CVT offline yet. Blocking it contained the risk; it didn't confirm the cause.
confidence.raiseIf: The offline capacitance test at the next clearance reads well off nameplate.
confidence.lowerIf: The bus voltage or a neighbouring bus starts moving with it. Then treat it as a real voltage problem.

action.text: Automatic voltage control using this CVT was blocked at 12:10 so the tap changer stops chasing a voltage that was never wrong. Replace the CVT at the next clearance; offline capacitance should be within 1–2 % of nameplate.

GSIT03.impact: Believed by automatic voltage control, a reading 6.2 % low would push the real bus voltage up by about that much, to roughly 1.056 pu, past the 1.05 pu limit.

conclusion.label: Cause
conclusion.text: Wyndham T1's voltage regulator was hunting: bandwidth too narrow for its tap step
conclusion.confidenceText: Confirmed: settled once the bandwidth was widened

chart.title: What we see
chart.caption: Tap operations per day on Wyndham T1 and on Aldergate T1. The regulated Wyndham 138 kV bus stayed inside its band the whole time.

checks.label: Tapping many times its normal rate
checks.value: Up to 57.5 operations/day at 12:00, against 4.6/day in the first hour (12×). The alert level here is 25/day.
checks.why: Each operation wears the diverter contacts. Normal tap changers in this fleet run 4–8 a day.

checks.label: Sustained, not a burst
checks.value: Above 25/day from 10:05 to 13:15.
checks.why: Needs 30 min, so a few quick taps to follow a real voltage step don't raise it.

checks.label: The voltage it regulates stayed in band
checks.value: Wyndham 138 kV bus held 0.982–1.003 pu while it hunted, inside 0.95–1.05 pu.
checks.why: A tap changer should only move when the voltage leaves its bandwidth. Nothing on the voltage display looked wrong, which is why this goes unnoticed.

checks.label: Tap position swinging back and forth
checks.value: 21 reversals between 10:05 and 13:10 (about 7 an hour), between taps −1 and 4, and it finished back where it started.
checks.why: Hunting raises, overshoots, lowers, overshoots. A tap changer following load moves one way.

checks.label: Another regulator moved in step
checks.value: Aldergate T1 tap changer rose from 6.6 to 13.1/day at 09:50 and back when this one settled.
checks.why: A separate counter on another transformer. Two regulators on the same voltage, fighting each other, both tap more.

checks.label: Settled after the settings change
checks.value: Widen Wyndham T1 regulator bandwidth at 12:45; below 20/day from 13:15 and 13.0/day now.
checks.why: Widening the bandwidth or lengthening the delay removed the overcorrection, and nothing in the network changed. That confirms the controls, not the voltage, were the cause.

references.title: Bandwidth narrower than two tap steps
references.description: One tap step moves the voltage further than the bandwidth, so every correction lands on the other side of the band. The rate jumps several-fold with the voltage in band, until the bandwidth is widened.
notes: Same jump with the voltage in band
Same drop once the setting was changed

references.title: Two paralleled regulators fighting
references.description: Two banks on the same voltage with mismatched settings or a failed paralleling scheme tap against each other, with circulating current between them. Both counters climb.
notes: Another tap changer rose in step here
Check the paralleling scheme as well as the bandwidth

references.title: Steep load ramp, healthy regulator
references.description: Load climbs fast and the voltage sags, so the tap changer steps up repeatedly, always the same way. Busy, but every operation is needed.
notes: Here the tap went back and forth
Here the voltage never needed it

ruledOut.reason: Wyndham 138 kV bus stayed at 0.982–1.003 pu. Its largest move today was −0.015 pu at 09:40, which one or two taps correct, not dozens.
Wyndham T1 load rose smoothly with the morning ramp; its largest 5-minute change while hunting was 1.0 points of loading.
The tap position itself swung between −1 and 4, and the operations counter gained 8 while it hunted.
The tap changer compartment stayed 4.5–5.1 °C below the main tank, and a settings change alone stopped it.

confidence.because: It tapped over ten times its normal rate with the voltage inside the band, and the rate fell back once the bandwidth and delay were widened, with nothing else changed.
confidence.lowerIf: The rate climbs again with the new settings. Then look at the paralleling scheme.
confidence.confirmedBy: Rate settled after the settings change

action.text: Bandwidth widened to 2.0 V at 12:45 and the time delay lengthened to 30 s. Review the paralleling scheme and the line-drop compensation settings before the next hot spell.

GSIT04.impact: At 58 operations/day a 75,000-operation maintenance interval lasts about 3.6 years instead of 44. A month of hunting at that rate is 1.0 years of normal wear.

conclusion.label: Cause
conclusion.text: Orrin–Larkspur 138 kV tripped on a fault, failed its reclose and is locked out

chart.title: What we see
chart.caption: MW flow on Orrin–Larkspur 138 kV at both ends, and the circuits that picked up its flow.

checks.label: Flow to zero in one scan, and stayed there
checks.value: 56.2 MW at 10:10, 0.0 MW at 10:15, and dead since: out 3 h 50 min now.
checks.why: A load can't drop 50 MW in five minutes on its own. The circuit opened.

checks.label: The breaker tripped, reclosed and tripped again
checks.value: Orrin breaker: reclose counter 9 → 10, operations 1,853 → 1,855, interrupting duty +3.84 kA²s.
checks.why: One reclose and two operations is trip, reclose, trip. Most line faults are temporary and clear on the reclose; this one was still there, so the relay locked out.

checks.label: The far end opened too
checks.value: Larkspur end: 55.0 MW → 0.0 MW in the same scan.
checks.why: A line fault trips both ends. One end open alone would point at that breaker or its relay.

checks.label: Voltage dipped at both ends in that scan
checks.value: Orrin 138 kV bus 0.063 pu, Larkspur 138 kV bus 0.058 pu, at 10:15 and back on the next scan. Every 138 kV and 69 kV bus that saw it dipped in the same scan, deepest at Orrin 138 kV bus, Larkspur 138 kV bus and Bexhill 138 kV bus.
checks.why: A separate measurement. A fault pulls the voltage down everywhere at once, deepest nearest the fault. Switching a healthy line out doesn't.

checks.label: Both breakers recorded it
checks.value: Larkspur breaker: reclose counter 3 → 4, operations +2.
checks.why: Two relays at two stations saw the same sequence, independently.

checks.label: The flow moved onto other circuits
checks.value: Bexhill–Orrin 138 kV 34 → 59 MW and Larkspur–Wexford 138 kV 30 → 48 MW in the same scan.
checks.why: Power divides by impedance: when a path opens, the parallel paths carry its flow at once.

references.title: Permanent fault: trip, reclose, lockout
references.description: Something stays on the line (a fallen conductor, a tree, damaged insulation). The reclose finds the fault still there, trips again and locks out until a patrol clears it.
notes: Flow to zero and staying there
One reclose, two operations, as here

references.title: Temporary fault, successful reclose
references.description: Lightning or a brief contact. The line trips and recloses within a second; the reclose counter steps but at five-minute scans the flow barely shows it.
notes: 85–95 % of line faults clear like this
Here the flow never came back (3 h 50 min)

references.title: Telemetry lost at one end
references.description: The RTU or its channel drops out and the flow freezes or reads zero at one end. The breaker counters don't move and the far end keeps reading load.
notes: Here both ends read zero
Here both breakers counted the sequence

ruledOut.reason: Both ends read zero, both breakers counted the operations, the buses dipped, and the other bays at Orrin kept reporting normally.
An operator opening a line doesn't add a reclose or a voltage dip. No switching on this circuit is in today's work list before the trip.
Both ends opened cleanly in the same scan and nothing else at either station lost its flow, so no breaker-failure protection operated.
The data can't say whether it was vegetation, lightning, contamination or damage. That is what the patrol is for; don't try to return the circuit until it reports.

confidence.because: The trip is recorded independently at both ends: both flows went to zero, both breakers counted trip, reclose, trip, and every nearby bus dipped in the same scan.
confidence.notHigherBecause: The lockout itself is certain; what caused the fault is not known until the patrol reports.
confidence.lowerIf: A breaker counter turns out to have been reset by maintenance. Then check the relay event reports.

action.text: Patrol between structures 41 and 78 first, where the fault locator puts it. Hold the restricted configuration until the circuit is back: the binding contingency is now the Wyndham–Larkspur circuit, not this one.

GSIT05.impact: The circuit is out of the contingency set. Worst post-contingency loading went from 61 % to 79 % at Orrin and 51 % to 105 % at Larkspur once its flow moved elsewhere.

conclusion.label: Cause
conclusion.text: Losing Orrin–Larkspur 138 kV put Larkspur one contingency from overload
conclusion.confidenceText: Relieved by switching, as the study predicted

chart.title: What we see

checks.why: Above 95 % the next single outage would take an element to its emergency rating; above 100 % it would overload it, an SOL exceedance that needs an operating plan.

checks.label: It jumped; load didn't creep there

checks.label: A circuit next to it went out in that scan
checks.value: Orrin–Larkspur 138 kV: 55.0 MW at 10:10, zero from 10:15, and still out.
checks.why: With that circuit gone, its flow and its role in the contingency set move to the paths that are left.

checks.value: Wyndham–Larkspur 138 kV 106 → 140 MW, Bexhill–Orrin 138 kV 34 → 59 MW and Larkspur–Wexford 138 kV 29 → 46 MW in the 10:15 scan.

checks.value: +3.6 points per hour over the last hour; 98.6 % now, which reaches 100 % again at about 14:28.
checks.why: The relief was a fixed amount of MW. The load ramp keeps adding to what is left.

references.title: Parallel path after a line loss
references.description: A circuit trips; its flow divides onto the parallel paths in the same scan, and the next contingency now overloads one of them. On 14 August 2003 each loss pushed the next line closer to its rating.
notes: A jump in one scan, with the circuit loss
Over the rating within minutes

references.title: Relieved by switching; the exposure moves
references.description: Closing a normally-open tie takes load off the stressed path. Flow divides by impedance, so part of it lands on a third element, and the load ramp takes the margin back.
notes: Navarre–Dunmore 69 kV tie closed at 11:25
Bexhill rose from 68 % to 97 %

references.title: Load growth to the limit
references.description: Post-contingency loading climbs a point or two an hour with the load until it meets the rating. No step, no element lost: the fix is dispatch, not switching.
notes: Here it jumped in one scan
Here a circuit went out at that moment

ruledOut.reason: Before the step it was rising +3.0 points an hour; the step was 39 points in 15 min.

action.text: Hold the restricted configuration and keep the tie closed until Orrin–Larkspur is back. Defer any switching in Harrow District that would take a second element out. Watch Bexhill T1, which is now the second most exposed element.

conclusion.label: Cause
conclusion.text: Wyndham 138 kV capacitor bank tripped at 09:40; Dunmore 69 kV bus sagged because that support was lost, 2 stations away
conclusion.confidenceText: Confirmed: voltage recovered when taps replaced the support

chart.title: What we see
chart.caption: Dunmore 69 kV bus against the other buses that sagged in the same scan, and the bus the capacitor bank sits on. The furthest bus sagged most.

checks.label: Below the pre-contingency floor
checks.value: Dunmore 69 kV bus 0.943 pu at its lowest; held at or under 0.95 pu from 09:40 to 10:35.
checks.why: System voltage should stay between 0.95 and 1.05 pu with everything in service. Below that, the next contingency starts from too low.

checks.label: It stepped down in one scan
checks.why: A step means something switched. Load growth pulls voltage down slowly.

checks.label: Reactive support was lost in the same scan
checks.value: Wyndham 138 kV capacitor bank: 49.2 MVAr at 09:35, 0.0 MVAr at 09:40. It is 2 stations away, via Larkspur.
checks.why: A shunt capacitor bank supplies reactive power locally. When it drops out, the MVAr has to come from further away, and voltage falls furthest where the network is weakest.

checks.label: The bank's own protection saw a failed can
checks.value: Neutral unbalance current 0.146 A before, 1.305 A from 09:40, and it stayed there.
checks.why: A separate measurement at the bank. A step that doesn't come back is a failed element and its fuse, not a drifting reading. The first failure alarms; the protection trips the bank.

checks.label: Sagged most far from the cause
checks.value: Same scan: Dunmore 69 kV bus 0.062, Larkspur 69 kV bus 0.045, Navarre 69 kV bus 0.026, Tilbury 69 kV bus 0.020, Larkspur 138 kV bus 0.019 pu; the bank's own Wyndham 138 kV bus 0.015 pu.
checks.why: Every bus saw it at once, deepest at the electrically weak end. The alarm is furthest from the cause.

checks.label: Nothing changed locally
checks.value: Load at Dunmore moved 1.5 % in that scan and every circuit there stayed in service.
checks.why: A local load step or a lost feed would also sag this bus, but only this bus and its neighbours.

checks.label: Recovered when taps were raised
checks.value: Larkspur T1 tap 2 → 4 and Colvin T1 tap 3 → 5 at 10:35; Dunmore 69 kV bus back above 0.95 pu by 10:40, 0.984 pu now.
checks.why: Raising taps restores voltage the way the lost MVAr would have. The bus answered, so reactive support was the problem; the bank still needs repair.

references.title: Capacitor bank trips on unbalance
references.description: A failed can blows its fuse, the unbalance protection trips the bank, and every bus nearby steps down in the same scan, the weak end of the network most. It holds there until support is restored.
notes: One-scan step, holding low, as here
Recovered with taps

references.title: A generator reaches its reactive limit
references.description: A nearby unit hits its over-excitation limit and stops supplying MVAr. Voltage slides over minutes instead of stepping, and the MVAr loss shows at the generator, not a bank.
notes: Here the voltage stepped
Here a bank lost its output

references.title: Fault dip, cleared
references.description: A fault anywhere nearby pulls every bus down for one scan; once it clears, the voltage comes straight back.
notes: Here it stayed low for 1 h
No reclose or trip at that time

ruledOut.reason: Load at Dunmore moved 1.5 % in that scan.
No circuit anywhere on the network lost its flow at 09:40.
The neighbouring buses sagged in the same scan, and this bus's CVT stayed within 0.36 % of its redundant partner.
That came at 10:15, 35 min after this sag began.

confidence.because: The sag, the bank's MVAr loss and its unbalance step are all in the same scan, the sag is deepest far from the bank, and the bus recovered once taps made up the support.
confidence.lowerIf: The voltage stays low with the taps raised. Then look for a second cause.
confidence.confirmedBy: Recovery after the taps were raised

action.text: Larkspur and Colvin taps were raised two steps at 10:35 as the interim fix. Inspect the bank, find the failed can, and re-baseline the inherent unbalance before returning it. Until then Wyndham and Thorne are short of reactive reserve.

GSIT07.impact: The taps are an interim fix; the 49 MVAr the bank supplied is still missing from the network's reactive reserve until it is repaired.

conclusion.label: Cause
conclusion.text: Repeated temporary faults at one place on Wexford–Tilbury 69 kV; the patrol found and cleared it
conclusion.confidenceText: Stopped after the patrol cleared it

chart.title: What we see
chart.caption: Successful auto-recloses on Wexford–Tilbury 69 kV. Each step is a fault the breaker cleared and reclosed through in under a second.

checks.label: 5 recloses in one shift
checks.value: Reclose counter 5 → 10: at 08:25, 09:15, 10:05, 11:10 and 12:00. The third came at 10:05, inside 4 h.
checks.why: One reclose is routine; most line faults are temporary. Several on the same circuit in a few hours is a cause that keeps coming back to the same place.

checks.label: Every reclose held
checks.value: Wexford–Tilbury 69 kV carried 17.8–22.3 MW in the scans of the events; no customer lost supply.

checks.label: The voltage dipped each time

checks.why: A separate measurement. Real faults pull the voltage down; a breaker opening on its own wouldn't.

checks.label: Breaker duty adding up
checks.value: Interrupting duty +2.10 kA²s and contact wear +1.8 points today, 48.8 % now.
checks.why: Every fault interruption erodes the contacts in proportion to the square of the current.

checks.label: Only this circuit
checks.value: None of the other 60 breakers counted a reclose at those times.
checks.why: A storm makes many circuits reclose within minutes. One circuit alone points at one place on it.

references.title: Vegetation growing into the line
references.description: On a hot afternoon the conductor sags with load and a limb makes contact every hour or so. Each fault clears on reclose until one doesn't. A patrol finds the tree.
notes: Steady run of successful recloses, one circuit
Stopped once the limb was cleared

references.title: Contamination flashover
references.description: Salt or dust on insulators flashes over when morning dew wets it. Events bunch early and stop as the day dries out.
notes: Here the events kept coming through midday
Insulator washing, not tree work, fixes it

references.title: Lightning storm passing
references.description: A storm front makes many circuits reclose within the same half hour, then nothing. It isn't a problem on any one circuit.
notes: Here no other circuit reclosed
Here the events were spread over 3 h 35 min

The bus voltage dipped at every event, which a breaker opening on its own wouldn't cause.
Wexford–Tilbury 69 kV was at 33 % of its normal rating at most.

confidence.lowerIf: Another reclose on this circuit today. Then the cause wasn't the one cleared.

action.text: The patrol found and cleared a limb contacting the B phase near structure 22 at 12:20. Keep the circuit on watch to end of shift and raise a vegetation work order for the span.

conclusion.label: Cause

checks.label: Past the hot-spot alert

checks.label: Exactly what its load and the weather predict

checks.label: All cooling running

checks.why: With every stage already on there is nothing left to switch in; the only lever left is load.

checks.why: A separate meter on the other bank. Identical banks in parallel should share load equally; a tap mismatch pushes more through one.

Here it fell as soon as the load did

Every line and transformer at Thorne is under 80 % of normal rating and the worst post-contingency loading is 67 %.
Thorne 345 kV bus is at 1.007 pu. The reserve is what is holding it there; the risk is the next contingency, not the present.

confidence.because: The reserve stepped in the same scan a capacitor bank at another station went to zero, other stations lost reserve at the same moment, and the station's own reactor then became committed.
confidence.notHigherBecause: The reserve is a derived figure, and the target is this utility's own. It hasn't been tested by returning the bank.
confidence.raiseIf: The reserve comes back by about the bank's rating when it returns to service.
confidence.lowerIf: A voltage-stability study shows enough margin at this reserve. Then the target is conservative for today.

action.text: Restore the Wyndham bank as the first priority — it is worth more here than any redispatch. Until then, treat a voltage event in Keldon or Harrow as unbacked, and pre-position the Thorne reactor out of service rather than in.

GSIT10.impact: 38 MVAr against a 120 MVAr target, with the evening peak still ahead. The next contingency starts with most of the voltage support already spent.

conclusion.label: Most likely cause
conclusion.text: A growing harmonic source at or below Colvin 69 kV bus, still under the limit

chart.title: What we see
chart.caption: Voltage THD at Colvin 69 kV bus and at the buses around it. The limit line is the conservative reading for this voltage class (see the rise check).

checks.label: Distortion well above its normal
checks.value: THD 2.05 % now against 0.96 % in the first hour (+1.09 points).
checks.why: Voltage distortion comes from harmonic currents drawn by nonlinear loads (drives, rectifiers, arc furnaces) flowing through the network impedance. The limit used here, 2.5 %, is IEEE 519's value for 69–161 kV buses; the standard puts a bus at exactly 69 kV in its 5 % class, so 2.5 % is the conservative reading.

checks.label: Still rising
checks.value: +0.25 points per hour over the last 2 h; rising since about 09:15.
checks.why: A source that is growing, not a one-off switching event.

checks.label: Held for hours
checks.value: More than 0.6 points above normal since 11:40.
checks.why: Needs 1 h, so a short burst from one load starting doesn't raise it.

checks.label: Negative-sequence voltage rising too
checks.value: 0.28 % in the first hour, 0.71 % now.
checks.why: A separate power-quality quantity. Large single-phase or unbalanced nonlinear loads raise both.

checks.label: Strongest here
checks.value: Rise since the first hour: Colvin 69 kV bus +1.09, Colvin 138 kV bus −0.09, Tilbury 69 kV bus +0.45 points.
checks.why: Distortion is worst nearest its source and weaker one circuit away. The bus above it at the same station staying flat puts the source below this bus, not on the transmission system.

checks.label: RMS voltage normal
checks.value: 0.993–1.005 pu all day.
checks.why: This is a waveform-quality problem, not a voltage-level problem; the voltage display shows nothing.

references.title: A nonlinear load growing on the feeder
references.description: A customer's drives or rectifiers ramp up with their production. Distortion climbs steadily through the day, strongest at the nearest bus.
notes: Steady climb, strongest here
Rising with the day, as here

references.title: A harmonic filter taken out of service
references.description: A customer's or the utility's filter bank trips or is switched out. THD steps up in one scan and holds.
notes: Here the rise was gradual

references.title: Resonance after capacitor switching
references.description: Switching a capacitor bank tunes the network near a harmonic; THD jumps while it is in, and drops when it comes out.
notes: No capacitor switching here today
Here it ramped

ruledOut.cause: Background distortion from the transmission system
ruledOut.reason: Colvin 138 kV bus at the same station moved −0.09 points.
Tilbury 69 kV bus rose too, by less (+0.45 points), and negative-sequence voltage moved here. One meter can't make its neighbours drift.
Resonance switches in and out with the bank. This rose smoothly over hours, and there is no shunt bank at this station.
The station transformer's loading moved 50 → 63 % while THD rose 2.1×. Ordinary load doesn't add distortion in proportion.

confidence.because: Distortion is rising steadily, strongest at this bus and weaker one circuit away, with negative-sequence voltage rising alongside.
confidence.notHigherBecause: The source is inferred from the gradient; nobody has surveyed the customers on this bus.
confidence.raiseIf: A power-quality survey finds the load, or the rise follows a customer's production pattern.
confidence.lowerIf: A second meter on the bus reads normal. Then check this one.

action.text: Put a power quality recorder on the Colvin 69 kV bus before the evening peak and contact the customer about filter status. If it reaches 2.5 % the limit is absolute regardless of who caused it.

GSIT11.impact: At +0.25 points per hour it reaches 2.5 % at about 15:54, around the evening peak.
